newsitem.title: USA: Four nations resume Korea talks.
newsitem.headline: Four nations resume Korea talks.

text.p: Famine-stricken North Korea resumed talks on Wednesday with the United States, South Korea and China to clear the way for negotiations intended to reach a permanent peace agreement on the divided Korean peninsula.
The preparatory talks, which began on Tuesday at Columbia University, have a limited purpose -- to set a date, time, place and agenda for the opening of formal negotiations, probably in September.

"We already have proposed two items for the agenda," said South Korean spokesman Yu Myang Hwan before the start of Wednesday's session. "Those are permanent mechanisms to replace the armistice and confidence building and tension reduction measures."
He said such measures could be worked out in the military, political and economic arenas. Yu said Seoul expected to have a "flexible mechanism" that need not necessarily be a formal peace treaty.
The goal was to replace the fraying armistice from the 1950-1953 Korean War with a more durable agreement, possibly in the form of a treaty.

U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam proposed the four-nation talks more than a year ago. It took months of discussions between Washington, Seoul and Pyongyang to reach the stage where China was also involved.

The meetings on Tuesday and Wednesday marked an important phase in the complex relationship between the four countries because it was the first time representatives of China had joined the talks. China is North Korea's ally and is a party to the armistice along with the United States and the two Koreas.
A U.S. State Department official said all indications were that "the so-called talks about talks" would not be completed on Wednesday.
Officials from all four delegations went to lunch without commenting on Wednesday morning's meeting.
One of the main obstacles has been North Korea's demand for food aid. The isolated Stalinist state has been struck by famine, drought and potential economic collapse.
U.N. agencies said on Monday that the drought had devasted 70 percent of the country's maize crop. The agency said even heavy rainfall would not be enough to alleviate the drought.
The United States and South Korea sought to keep food aid out of the peace talks, but Pyongyang raised the matter in previous meetings during the past year.
"The United States is not linking the issue of food to these talks," a senior State Department official said. "We are willing to respond to appeals through the United Nations World Food Programme."
The official said Tuesday's first session was described by the Washington delegation as "businesslike."
The World Food Programme made a fresh appeal last month for $46 million in food aid for North Korea in addition to an earlier request of $95.5 million.

On the eve of the four-nation talks in New York, there were a series of conciliatory steps taken on the tense Korean peninsula, the last flashpoint of the Cold War. In the 1950-1953 Korean conflict, the United States backed the capitalist South and China supported the communist North.

Monday, Pyongyang handed over the remains of four U.S. soldiers killed in the war and the two Koreas linked up their public telephone lines for the first time since 1945. The Red Cross of South Korea also announced food supplies to the North.
